subject: Vocabulary
topic: Commonly confused words II — mixed tiers
description: Word pairs often misused in writing

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The new policy will ___ a major change.'
questions.explanation: 'Effect' as a verb means 'to bring about / cause'. 'The policy will effect a change' = will bring about a change. 'Affect' (verb) = influence — 'The policy will affect workers.' 'Effect' as a noun = result. 'Affluent' = wealthy (adj.); 'effluent' = outflowing waste water.
questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.topic: Commonly confused words II — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'Who is the lead ___ in the play?'
questions.explanation: 'Principal' (n/adj) — main, chief; head of a school; a lead actor. 'Principle' (noun only) — a rule or standard of conduct. Memory aid — 'The princiPAL is your PAL' (for the school meaning). 'Prescient' = having foresight; 'precedent' = an earlier case used as a model. These sound similar but are unrelated.
questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.topic: Commonly confused words II — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'Please ___ me of your decision.'
questions.explanation: 'Advise' (verb, pronounced ad-VIZE) = to give counsel, inform. 'Advice' (noun, pronounced ad-VICE) = counsel given. 'I advise you to take my advice.' Memory aid — advi-S-e is the verb (s for 'say'), advi-C-e is the noun. 'Advent' = arrival; 'adverse' = unfavourable — unrelated.
questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.topic: Commonly confused words II — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The ___ of the report is alarming.'
questions.explanation: 'Content' = what a report, book, speech contains (the substance / subject matter). 'Complement' = something that completes or matches (a compliment to one's wardrobe). 'Compliment' = a polite expression of praise. 'Contempt' = disdain; scorn. Here — the substance of the report — 'content'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.topic: Commonly confused words II — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'Everyone was present ___ the chairman.'
questions.explanation: 'Except' (prep/conj) = excluding. 'Everyone except the chairman' = everyone other than the chairman. 'Accept' (verb) = receive willingly — 'I accept your apology.' Memory — EX-cept excludes (Ex = out); AC-cept accepts something in. 'Exact' = precise; 'expect' = anticipate — unrelated spellings that sometimes get mixed.
questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.topic: Commonly confused words II — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The weather has had a serious ___ on the crops.'
questions.explanation: 'Effect' as a noun = the result of an action or cause. 'A serious effect on the crops' = a serious result. 'Affect' is almost always a verb — 'the weather has affected the crops.' Swap them carefully — 99 % of use follows 'affect = verb, effect = noun'. Exceptions — 'to effect a change' (verb, bring about) and 'flat affect' (noun, psychological term) are rare.
questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.topic: Commonly confused words II — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The doctor prescribed a new ___ for the patient.'
questions.explanation: 'Medicine' = drug / substance used to treat illness. 'Meditation' = mental practice for calm / focus. 'Mediation' = third-party intervention to settle a dispute. 'Medium' = a means / intermediate agent (a medium of communication). Four similar-sounding words with very different meanings — classic exam confusable set.

questions.topic: Commonly confused words II — mixed tiers

questions.stem: The school principal issued a notice asking parents to ensure that every student carries adequate ___ for the practical examination next week.

options.option_text: stationery — pens, pencils, erasers, and notebooks
stationary — objects that remain unmoved or fixed
statutory — items required under provisions of law
signatory — a person authorised to sign agreements

questions.explanation: 'Stationery' (noun) refers to writing and office materials such as pens, paper, and notebooks. The classic distractor 'stationary' is an adjective meaning not moving or fixed in place — a spelling-trap since both words are homophones. 'Statutory' and 'signatory' are phonetically dissimilar but test whether the candidate reads carefully.

questions.stem: The architect insisted on following the ___ of load distribution while designing the multi-storey residential complex.

options.option_text: principal — denoting the most important key person
principled — meaning guided by strong moral values
principle — denoting a fundamental rule or concept
precedent — denoting a prior ruling or legal example

questions.explanation: 'Principle' is a noun meaning a fundamental truth, rule, or governing concept — load distribution is an engineering principle. 'Principal' is the most seductive distractor; it can mean the head of an institution or the primary component, but it cannot mean a rule or guiding idea. 'Principled' is an adjective and does not fit the article 'the' followed by 'of'.

questions.stem: The mining company was penalized Rs 50 lakh for brazenly ___ the environmental clearance norms prescribed by the State Pollution Control Board.

options.option_text: flouting — openly defying and disregarding the rules
flagging — marking or drawing attention to concerns
evading — cleverly side-stepping the regulations set

questions.explanation: 'Flout' means to openly disobey or show contempt for a rule or convention — exactly what the company did with environmental norms. 'Flaunt', the classic distractor, means to display something boastfully; it carries no sense of rule-breaking, yet many test-takers (and writers) erroneously use it in place of 'flout'. Penalization presupposes violation, confirming that rule-defiance is the target meaning.

questions.stem: The research paper classified soil erosion into three ___ categories, each governed by different causal mechanisms and remediation strategies.

options.option_text: discreet — careful and circumspect in one's behaviour
discrete — individually separate and mutually distinct
diffuse — spread loosely over a very wide surface area
discernible — able to be perceived or recognised clearly

questions.explanation: 'Discrete' means individually separate and non-overlapping — the three categories are self-contained units, which is precisely this word's meaning. 'Discreet' is the most tempting distractor because both words are homophones; however, 'discreet' means tactful or careful to avoid embarrassment, a meaning wholly irrelevant in a scientific context. 'Discernible' means perceptible and does not describe classification structure.

questions.stem: The finance ministry's report noted that commercial vehicles tend to ___ more sharply than residential property owing to intensive utilisation and maintenance costs.

options.option_text: deprecate — to express formal disapproval or censure
depreciate — to lose monetary value progressively over time
degenerate — to decline to a significantly lower quality
deteriorate — to become progressively worse in condition

questions.explanation: 'Depreciate' is the standard accounting and financial term for a decrease in asset value over time — exactly what the context demands. 'Deprecate' is the key distractor: it means to express disapproval (and in software, to phase out a feature), but it has no sense of monetary loss. Candidates who know 'mitigating depreciation' from commerce often muddle the two verbs.

questions.stem: The panel member's pointed question about the undisclosed off-balance-sheet liability visibly ___ the auditor, who struggled to maintain composure before the committee.

options.option_text: discomforted — caused a mild sense of physical unease
discomfited — unnerved and thrown into mental confusion
disconcerted — left briefly unsettled or only mildly disturbed
dismayed — filled with a sudden overwhelming sense of gloom

questions.explanation: 'Discomfit' means to thoroughly unsettle or baffle someone, causing acute loss of composure in a formal or public setting — precisely what happens to the auditor. 'Discomfort' (→ discomforted) denotes physical or mild emotional unease, not the sharp mental confusion implied here. 'Disconcerted' is close but lacks the intensity and public-embarrassment connotation that 'discomfited' carries, making it the wrong choice despite being a near-synonym.

questions.stem: The defence counsel argued that the accused's decade-long record of pro-bono legal aid should ___ in his favour when the court determines the quantum of punishment.

options.option_text: mitigate — to reduce the severity or intensity overall
mediate — to act as an impartial third-party negotiator
militate — to be a compelling factor influencing the outcome
moderate — to make the punishment less extreme in degree

questions.explanation: 'Militate' (followed by 'in favour of' or 'against') means to be a powerful factor that actively works toward a result — the correct legal idiom. 'Mitigate' is the most seductive distractor: while 'mitigating circumstances' is standard legal vocabulary, the construction 'mitigate in his favour' is ungrammatical; you mitigate a sentence or severity, not a verdict direction. The distinction requires precise awareness of complementation patterns, not just word meaning.
